{{Short description|Polyhedron related to sphere packing}}

{{more footnotes|date=November 2013}}
{{more citations|date=April 2023}}

In [[geometry]], the '''Waterman polyhedra''' are a family of [[polyhedron|polyhedra]] discovered around 1990 by the mathematician [[Steve Waterman (mathematician)|Steve Waterman]]. A Waterman polyhedron is created by [[Sphere packing|packing spheres]] according to the [[cubic close packing|cubic close(st) packing]] (CCP), also known as the face-centered cubic (fcc) packing, then sweeping away the spheres that are farther from the center than a defined radius,<ref name=Popko2012>{{cite book|last=Popko|first=Edward S.|title=Divided Spheres: Geodesics and the Orderly Subdivision of the Sphere|year=2012|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781466504295|pages=174–177}}</ref> then creating the [[convex hull]] of the sphere centers.

Image:Waterman_Packed_Spheres_0024.1.png|Cubic Close(st) Packed spheres with radius {{sqrt|24}}
Image:Waterman_0024.1.png|Corresponding Waterman polyhedron W24 Origin 1
</gallery>
[[File:W5 sphere cluster.jpg|thumb|Waterman/fcc sphere cluster W5]]
[[File:W5 polyhedron.jpg|thumb|Waterman/fcc polyhedra interpretation of sphere cluster w5]]
Waterman polyhedra form a vast family of polyhedra. Some of them have a number of special properties such as multiple symmetries, or interesting and regular shapes. Others are less structured collection of faces formed from irregular [[convex polygon]]s.

The most popular Waterman polyhedra are those with centers at the point (0,0,0) and built out of hundreds of polygons. Such polyhedra resemble spheres. In fact, the more faces a Waterman polyhedron has, the more it resembles its [[circumscribed sphere]] in volume and total area.

With each point of 3D space we can associate a family of Waterman polyhedra with different values of radii of the circumscribed spheres. Therefore, from a mathematical point of view we can consider Waterman polyhedra as 4D spaces W(x, y, z, r), where x, y, z are coordinates of a point in 3D, and r is a positive number greater than 1.<ref>[http://www.mupad.com/mathpad/2006/majewski/index.php Visualizing Waterman Polyhedra with MuPAD] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080112025536/http://www.mupad.com/mathpad/2006/majewski/index.php |date=2008-01-12 }} by M. Majewski</ref>

==Seven origins of cubic close(st) packing (CCP)==

There can be seven origins defined in CCP,<ref>[http://dogfeathers.com/java/ccppoly.html 7 Origins of CCP Waterman polyhedra] by Mark Newbold</ref> where n = {1, 2, 3, …}:
* Origin 1: offset 0,0,0, radius <math>\sqrt{2n}</math>
* Origin 2: offset {{sfrac|1|2}},{{sfrac|1|2}},0, radius <math>\tfrac12\sqrt{2+4n}</math>
* Origin 3: offset {{sfrac|1|3}},{{sfrac|1|3}},{{sfrac|2|3}}, radius <math>\tfrac13\sqrt{6(n+1)}</math>
* Origin 3*: offset {{sfrac|1|3}},{{sfrac|1|3}},{{sfrac|1|3}}, radius <math>\tfrac13\sqrt{3+6n}</math>
* Origin 4: offset {{sfrac|1|2}},{{sfrac|1|2}},{{sfrac|1|2}}, radius <math>\tfrac12\sqrt{3+8(n-1)}</math>
* Origin 5: offset 0,0,{{sfrac|1|2}}, radius <math>\tfrac12\sqrt{1+4n}</math>
* Origin 6: offset 1,0,0, radius <math>\sqrt{1+2(n-1)}</math>

Depending on the origin of the sweeping, a different shape and resulting polyhedron are obtained.

==Relation to Platonic and Archimedean solids==
{{Unsourced section|date=April 2023}}

Some Waterman polyhedra create [[Platonic solid]]s and [[Archimedean solid]]s. For this comparison of Waterman polyhedra they are normalized, e.g. {{nowrap|W2 O1}} has a different size or volume than {{nowrap|W1 O6,}} but has the same form as an octahedron.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

===Platonic solids===
*Tetrahedron: W1 O3*, W2 O3*, W1 O3, W1 O4
*Octahedron: W2 O1, W1 O6
*Cube: W2 O6
*Icosahedron and dodecahedron have no representation as Waterman polyhedra.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

===Archimedean solids===
*[[Cuboctahedron]]: W1 O1, W4 O1
*[[Truncated octahedron]]: W10 O1
*[[Truncated tetrahedron]]: W4 O3, W2 O4
*The other Archimedean solids have no representation as Waterman polyhedra.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

The W7 O1 might be mistaken for a [[truncated cuboctahedron]], as well W3 O1 = W12 O1 mistaken for a [[rhombicuboctahedron]], but those Waterman polyhedra have two edge lengths and therefore do not qualify as Archimedean solids.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

==Generalized Waterman polyhedra==
{{Unsourced section|date=April 2023}}
Generalized Waterman polyhedra are defined as the convex hull derived from the point set of any spherical extraction from a regular lattice.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

Included is a detailed analysis of the following 10 lattices – bcc, cuboctahedron, diamond, fcc, hcp, truncated octahedron, [[rhombic dodecahedron]], simple cubic, truncated tet tet, truncated tet truncated octahedron cuboctahedron.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

Each of the 10 lattices were examined to isolate those particular origin points that manifested a unique polyhedron, as well as possessing some minimal symmetry requirement.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}} From a viable origin point, within a lattice, there exists an unlimited series of polyhedra.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}} Given its proper sweep interval, then there is a one-to-one correspondence between each [[Integer-valued polynomial|integer value]] and a generalized Waterman polyhedron.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}
